observation: Rozenblit & Keil (2002) found people systematically overrate their explanatory understanding of everyday mechanisms far more than their factual/procedural/narrative knowledge, and the illusion collapses when they're forced to generate an explanation themselves.
claim: An AI-generated summary that the user only reads (never generates) risks leaving an illusion of explanatory depth that a self-generated explanation would have punctured.
mechanism: Understanding-illusion is specifically about explanatory depth and is corrected only by the act of generating an explanation, not by re-reading one.

implications.text: Avoid UI language implying 'you now understand X' after a passive L0/L1 read; reserve 'understand' framing for after a generative or retrieval-check interaction.

observation: Thiede & Dunlosky's metacomprehension research shows immediate felt-understanding judgments are poorly correlated with test performance, but generating keywords or a summary after a delay (not immediately) reliably improves the accuracy of that self-judgment.
claim: A delayed (not immediate) generative check is a stronger metacomprehension-calibration mechanism than an immediate one.
mechanism: Delay forces reliance on the durable situation-model representation rather than fading surface/perceptual memory.

implications.text: If a retrieval-check or self-summary prompt is shown, insert a beat/delay before it rather than firing immediately after the content, per the delayed-keyword effect.

observation: Lee et al. (2025, CHI, Microsoft Research/CMU) surveyed 319 knowledge workers on 936 AI use cases: self-reported critical-thinking effort was lower when confidence in the AI's ability was higher, and higher when confidence in one's own ability was higher.
claim: A static 'AI-generated, may contain errors' disclaimer is unlikely to change scrutiny; trust in the tool and trust in oneself pull critical-thinking effort in opposite directions, and this is a behavioral-attention problem, not an information problem.
mechanism: Attention allocation to verification is driven by relative confidence in the tool versus oneself, not by explicit warnings.

implications.text: Replace passive disclaimers with an active, specific factual prequestion or retrieval-check drawn from L2/L3 content, which changes attention allocation rather than just asserting a warning.

observation: Vasconcelos et al. (CHI 2023, 731 participants across 5 studies) found explanations attached to AI output reduce overreliance only when they lower the cost of independently verifying the claim; otherwise explanations become a trust heuristic people lean on without verifying, increasing overreliance.
claim: A source-span hover/highlight only calibrates trust if it lets the user genuinely judge the claim in a few seconds (a full sentence or two of source text); a citation marker alone risks becoming a false trust cue.
mechanism: An explanation's value depends on whether it actually lowers verification cost, not on its mere presence.

implications.text: Hover/expand on a summary claim must show enough source text (a full sentence or two of L3) for genuine verification in under ~5 seconds, not just a citation marker.

observation: Buçinca, Malaya & Gajos (2021, CHI/CSCW, 199 participants) found cognitive forcing functions (commit to your own answer before seeing the AI's) significantly reduce overreliance, but the forcing functions that reduced overreliance most also received the least favorable satisfaction ratings, and benefited high-Need-for-Cognition users more.
claim: Predict-before-reveal / cognitive forcing works to reduce false fluency but is disliked and not uniformly effective, so it must be opt-in/occasional rather than a default constant friction.
mechanism: Forcing commitment before revealing an answer interrupts automatic reliance, but the added friction itself costs subjective satisfaction.

implications.text: Make predict-before-reveal skip-optional and suggested only occasionally (e.g. once per document, or when a skim-then-bail pattern is detected), not on every zoom transition.

observation: DiSCo (2026 preprint) found a summarization interface that explicitly surfaces content the source implies but the summary omits was rated significantly more detailed and decision-useful (d=0.62) at a moderate cost to perceived ease of understanding (d=0.51); the authors recommend concise-by-default with omission detail on secondary interaction.
claim: A single collapsed 'this summary skips: [X]' line at L1/L2, expandable on demand, is a directly evidenced (if preliminary) pattern for surfacing what an abstraction level leaves out.
mechanism: Explicitly naming expected-but-omitted content gives users a concrete signal of what the summary is not covering, without requiring them to already know what's missing.

implications.text: Generate a single collapsed 'this level leaves out' line by diffing L1/L2 against L3, default-collapsed with expand-on-tap, not shown in full by default.

observation: Parasuraman & Manzey's (2010) foundational review found automation bias — following an automated recommendation against one's own better judgment — is not reliably prevented by training or disclaimers alone, and affects experts and novices roughly equally; the mechanism is misallocated attention, not a discrete belief.
claim: Structural friction (forced commitment, visible cost of trust), not informational warnings, is the only reliable lever against automation bias.
mechanism: Automation bias is an attentional allocation failure, so adding information (a warning label) does not change where attention goes.
population: general adults, experts and novices (human-automation-interaction review)
context: foundational review across decades of research

implications.text: Do not rely on a static 'AI-generated' disclaimer as a trust-calibration mechanism; use structural mechanisms (forcing functions, verification-lowering hover) instead.

observation: No study was found directly comparing 'read an AI abstraction-tree/summary' vs. 'read the original' on later comprehension and retention — the closest adjacent evidence (generation effect, metacomprehension, AI-and-writing studies) supports related but not identical claims.
claim: Riemann's core bet — that the zoom dial reaches real understanding faster than reading the original — is currently supported only by adjacent evidence, not a direct test of the exact task; Riemann should treat this as an open, testable hypothesis.
mechanism: N/A — this is an evidence-gap observation, not a mechanistic claim.
context: evidence gap, flagged explicitly by the report

implications.text: Instrument Riemann itself (confidence-vs-correctness gaps, verification follow-through) to test the abstraction tree's comprehension benefit directly, rather than assuming adjacent evidence transfers.
